title: Rethinking Temporal Consistency in Video Object-Centric Learning: From Prediction to Correspondence
claim: Prior methods learn expensive predictors to keep object identity over time; ours replaces them with parameter-free discrete matching.
layout: 2 stacked panels (blue vs orange), left-to-right flow, shared frozen-backbone input at left
description: A shared input on the left shows video frames 0, 1 and t entering a frozen DINOv2 encoder, drawn as a trapezoid with a snowflake icon. The output features X feed two horizontal bands. The top, blue 'Predictive Paradigm' band runs left to right: content-blind initialization (a Gaussian curve and '?' boxes), then Slot Attention, then a learned predictor drawn as a neural network (GRU or Transformer), then Next Frame Slot Attention. It is captioned 'Dynamic Modeling, High Computational Cost'. The bottom, orange 'Grounded Correspondence Paradigm' band runs the same way: a saliency heatmap with colored query squares, Slot Attention, then Hungarian Correspondence, shown as a bipartite graph and a cost matrix. It is captioned 'Discrete Matching, Zero Learnable Parameters'. Arrows are labeled with math symbols such as Q, S and X. The blue and orange contrast draws the eye first.
caption: From prediction to correspondence: rethinking temporal consistency in video object-centric learning. Top: The predictive paradigm uses content-blind initialization without spatial priors. Temporal consistency relies on learned dynamics modules that forecast future slot states through high-capacity Transformers [ref] or recurrent networks [ref]. Bottom: Grounded Correspondence eliminates learned temporal parameters entirely. Slots initialize from saliency peaks in frozen backbone features. Frame-to-frame identity is maintained through parameter-free Hungarian matching [ref] on slot representations. This paradigm shift achieves competitive performance with zero learnable parameters for temporal modeling.
abstract: The de facto approach in video object-centric learning maintains temporal consistency through learned dynamics modules that predict future object representations, called slots. We demonstrate that these predictors function as expensive approximations of discrete correspondence problems. Modern self-supervised vision backbones already encode instance-discriminative features that distinguish objects reliably. Exploiting these features eliminates the need for learned temporal prediction. We introduce Grounded Correspondence, a framework that replaces learned transition functions with deterministic bipartite matching. Slots initialize from salient regions in frozen backbone features. Frame-to-frame identity is maintained through Hungarian matching on slot representations. The approach requires zero learnable parameters for temporal modeling yet achieves competitive performance on MOVi-D, MOVi-E, and YouTube-VIS.
